title: Powering ISRU plants: the megawatt gap
bottleneck: Serious ISRU — melting regolith, electrolyzing water, liquefying propellant — needs megawatts of continuous power, but a lunar base's early power will be kilowatts. Solar at the poles works only on crater rims with near-constant sunlight and still needs storage; nuclear fission surface power is the natural answer but is itself undeployed. The power system must be landed, installed, and operational before the ISRU plant produces its first kilogram — and it dominates the landed mass budget.
why_it_blocks: Power is the master constraint: every ISRU mass and throughput estimate collapses without a credible megawatt source, yet power and ISRU are usually planned as separate programs.
current_state: Kilopower demonstrated the 10 kW class; a 40 kW lunar fission demo is targeted for the early 2030s. Megawatt-class surface power has no program.
